pages.text: The school bus stopped beside the river. Madam Asamoah stepped out with a seedling in a pot. “Today,” she said, “we imagine the same river twenty years from now. Benewaa, you are thirteen. In twenty years you will be thirty-three. What kind of river will you have?” Benewaa looked at the brown water. “That depends,” she said, “on what we do.”

pages.text: “Let us look at the first future,” said Madam Asamoah. “Imagine nothing changes. The river stays brown. Water plants shut down more often and families buy water from tankers. Farms become pits. The fish are gone. Children grow up on poisoned water. Young men dig in dangerous pits and some do not come out. A few people grow rich. Most do not.”

pages.alt: A grey picture of a dry brown river, empty fishing boats, and a long queue at a water tanker.

pages.text: “Now the second future,” she went on. “Imagine that people do their part. Mining happens only on licensed land, with safe methods and rules that are kept. The banks are replanted. The fish return. The treatment plants run smoothly. Farms are green. Young people have jobs in farming, crafts, tree planting and clean mining. Scientists estimate that healing rivers could take ten to twenty years of steady work.”

pages.text: “Is that possible?” asked Dakurah. “It has happened elsewhere,” said Madam Asamoah. “One editorial notes that the Rhine in Europe was called biologically dead in the 1970s and now supports life again, after money, laws and years of enforcement. The Singapore River was cleaned in ten years. Neither is the same as ours, but each shows that rivers can recover when people decide to heal them.”

pages.text: “So who has to do what?” asked Benewaa. Madam Asamoah handed out cards. “Let us write promises,” she said. “Not slogans. Promises that someone can keep. Let us start with those who lead.” Benewaa wrote for the Minister: “I will publish monthly river readings and prosecute financiers as well as diggers.” For the Assembly Member: “I will clear drains, protect banks and tell the town what I have done.”

pages.text: Dakurah wrote for the chief: “I will protect the river and the farms and pass a bylaw.” For the farmer: “I will refuse to rent my land to illegal miners and plant a tree for every tree lost.” For the miner: “I will seek a licence, use safe methods and never use child labour.” For the journalist: “I will report fairly and check my facts.” For the doctor: “I will test and treat children and tell the truth about what we find.”

pages.alt: A pupil writes more promise cards at a table, each one pinned beneath a drawing of a different villager.

pages.text: Last, they wrote their own promises. Benewaa wrote: “I will never throw rubbish in a drain or river. I will ask questions and check facts.” Dakurah wrote: “I will plant a tree each year and tell my family the truth about water.” Madam Asamoah wrote: “I will teach, and I will never stop asking leaders for answers.” She added: “And I will remember that no single person can fix this, but everyone can do something.”

pages.alt: A teacher and two pupils pin their promise cards to a banner beside the river.

pages.text: They planted the seedling together on the bank, in a spot far from the water’s edge. Madam Asamoah took a photo. “In twenty years,” she said, “let us come back and take the same photo.” Dakurah grinned. “I will be thirty-three. I will bring my own children.” Benewaa looked at the brown river, then at the tiny tree. “And we will tell them,” she said, “that we started today.” The end.

activities.question: How long might it take rivers to recover, according to the story?

activities.question: What do Benewaa and Dakurah promise to do?
options: Not litter, ask questions, plant a tree and tell the truth
